### Exercise 1: Estimating with Confidence Intervals

**Calculate the 95% confidence intervals for the mean values of the variables `height` and `mortstat`.**

💡 SPSS:

<div class="instruction-flow">
<span class="text-steps">Step 1: </span>
  <span class="step">Analyze</span>
  <span class="arrow">→</span>
  <span class="step">Descriptive Statistics</span>
    <span class="arrow">→</span>
  <span class="step">Explore</span>
</div> 

<span class="text-steps">Step 2: </span> Assign `height` and `mortstat` as dependent variables.

<span class="text-steps">Step 3: </span> Under "Display", select "Statistics".

<span class="text-steps">Step 4: </span> In the "Statistics" menu, set the desired confidence interval limits.

<span class="text-steps">Step 5: </span> Under "Options", choose "Exclude cases pairwise".

![](CI.png)

<details>

<summary>Show Results</summary>

| **Variable**   | **Mean (95% Confidence Intervals)** | 
|:---------------|:------------------------------------|
| height         |   167.05 (166.89 - 167.21)          | 
| mortstat       |   0.26 (0.25 - 0.27)                |

</details>

**Comprehension question about Confidence Intervals:**

Which statement do you agree with:

a) For a 95% confidence interval, the true population value lies within the limits of the interval with a probability of 95%.

b) A 95% confidence interval means that if multiple samples are drawn, 95% of the resulting intervals will contain the true population value. Whether the confidence interval contains the true value in an individual case cannot be determined.

<details>

<summary>Show Results</summary>

 ✓ `b) A 95% confidence interval means that if multiple samples are drawn, 95% of the resulting intervals will contain the true population value. Whether the confidence interval contains the true value in an individual case cannot be determined.`

</details>

### Exercise 2: Testing for normality

In the lecture, you learned about different ways to test for normality. In brief, these are:

1) Assessment of skewness and kurtosis (kurtosis should be 3 – describes the steepness/peakedness of the distribution)

2) Statistical tests for normality

3) Graphical tests for normality

Knowledge about the distribution of variables can, among other things, help in selecting the appropriate test.

**Check the variables `height`, `bmi`, and `cal_mean` for normality.**

💡 SPSS:

<div class="instruction-flow">
<span class="text-steps">Step 1: </span>
  <span class="step">Analyze</span>
  <span class="arrow">→</span>
  <span class="step">Descriptive Statistics</span>
    <span class="arrow">→</span>
  <span class="step">Explore</span>
</div> 

<span class="text-steps">Step 2: </span> Under "Display", select "Both".

<span class="text-steps">Step 3: </span> In the "Statistics" menu, set the desired confidence interval limits.

<span class="text-steps">Step 4: </span> Under "Plots", choose "Normality plots with tests" and "Histogram".

<span class="text-steps">Step 5: </span> Assign `height`, `bmi`, and `cal_mean` as dependent variables.

**For `height`, `bmi`, and `cal_mean`, test for normal distribution graphically by examining their histograms and Q-Q plots.** 

Determine which of the variables can be assumed to follow a normal distribution.

![](Normality_test.png){width=80%}

</details>

| bmi            |   No                    | 

</details>
